meta_description: Learn what epoxy is: how the two-part resin cures, its key properties, the main resin types and where epoxy is used in manufacturing and composites.
monitored_text: Key summary Epoxy is a two-part thermosetting polymer. A resin and a hardener cure into a rigid, chemically resistant solid that cannot be remelted. It bonds to metals, glass, ceramics, wood and composites, resists moisture and insulates electrically. Unless toughened it is brittle, and it degrades under UV exposure. The main resin types are: Bisphenol-A: general-purpose bonding Bisphenol-F: lower viscosity and better chemical resistance Novolac: high-temperature and chemically aggressive environments Epoxy is used as a structural adhesive, a protective coating, an electronic potting compound and the matrix in fiber-reinforced composites such as FR4 circuit board laminates. It only reaches its rated properties with an accurate mix ratio and a full cure. Uncured resin is a skin sensitizer, but fully cured epoxy is generally considered safe. This guide covers epoxy’s properties, compares the main resin types, outlines manufacturing applications including composite layup, and explains processing, curing and safety considerations. What is epoxy? Epoxy forms when an epoxide resin cures with a hardener. The reaction creates a cross-linked network, so once epoxy sets it cannot be melted or reshaped. This is what separates a thermoset from a thermoplastic , which softens when heated and can be remelted. Epoxy is familiar as a craft and coating resin, but engineering grades are made for structural loads, high service temperatures and harsh chemical environments. What is epoxy made of? Epoxy is a two-part system. It consists of a resin and a hardener, sometimes called a curing agent. On their own, both elements stay liquid and stable, so they can be stored for long periods before use. Mixed in the correct ratio, the elements trigger a chemical reaction called cross-linking, where the molecules bond into a dense three-dimensional network. That reaction gives off heat and is irreversible. The liquid thickens and hardens into a rigid solid, so getting the mix ratio right matters more than with most glues or paints. Properties of epoxy Epoxy is valued for a set of properties that few single materials combine. It bonds strongly to metals, glass, wood and many plastics, which makes it a versatile structural adhesive. It also resists chemicals and moisture, so it holds up in harsh service environments. On top of that, epoxy has good electrical insulation. This is a key reason it appears throughout electronics. It stays dimensionally stable and shrinks very little as it cures, so bonded and cast parts keep their shape. The main trade-offs are limited UV stability in some formulations and brittleness unless the resin is toughened. Types of epoxy resin Most engineering epoxies come from a few resin chemistries, and the differences show up in heat and chemical resistance. The most common is bisphenol-A, the workhorse, offering a balance of strength, adhesion and cost for general use. Bisphenol-F has lower viscosity and better chemical resistance, which suits coatings and demanding environments. A third type, novolac, carries more reactive sites, so it cross-links more densely and withstands higher temperatures and aggressive chemicals. Choosing between them comes down to how hot and how chemically harsh the application gets. What is epoxy used for in manufacturing? In manufacturing, epoxy fills several distinct roles. It works as a structural adhesive for bonding metals and composites where welding or fasteners are impractical and as a protective coating that resists abrasion and chemicals on floors and equipment. It also seals electronic components in a protective layer to shield them from moisture and vibration. One of its most familiar uses is the resin in printed circuit board substrates, most notably FR4 . This is a glass-reinforced epoxy laminate that machines into rigid, electrically insulating parts. Epoxy as a composite matrix Epoxy is the most common matrix for high-performance composites, the material that surrounds and binds the reinforcing fibers. When combined with glass, carbon, or aramid fibers, it transfers load between the fibers and holds them in the designed orientation. The fibers carry the tensile and bending loads, while the epoxy keeps them aligned, protects them and resists compression. This combination produces parts with a high strength-to-weight ratio. This is why epoxy composites, for example, appear in aerospace , automotive and sporting goods where weight matters. Working with epoxy: Processing, curing and safety Epoxy is processed as a liquid, then cured to a solid. This curing can happen at room temperature or be accelerated with heat. The cure schedule affects the final strength and heat resistance, so following the manufacturer's ratios and times is essential. Uncured epoxy resins and hardeners can irritate skin and airways. Repeated contact can cause sensitization. Always work in a ventilated area, wear gloves and eye protection and avoid skin contact. Once fully cured, epoxy is safe to handle, which is why finished parts pose little risk. How to choose the right epoxy The right epoxy depends on the job. For general bonding, a bisphenol-A resin gives good strength at low cost, while jobs involving heat or aggressive chemicals point toward novolac grades that hold up under those conditions. Match the cure speed to your task as well. A fast-curing epoxy suits small repairs, but a slower cure gives the working time needed for large laminating or casting jobs. Do you work with structural and load-bearing parts? Confirm the mechanical and thermal ratings against the application before committing to a resin. You're now subscribed to our newsletter. Frequently asked questions What is the difference between epoxy and resin? Resin is the general term for a liquid that cures into a solid. Epoxy is one specific type, cured with a hardener through cross-linking. So all epoxy is resin, but not all resin is epoxy; polyester and polyurethane resins are other examples. How long does epoxy take to cure? It depends on the formulation and the temperature. Fast-curing epoxies can set in minutes, while structural and laminating grades may take hours and heat speeds the process up. Full strength is usually reached over a day or more. Is epoxy stronger than glue? For structural bonds, epoxy is generally stronger and more durable than most common glues, and it bonds well to metals , glass and composites. That is why it is chosen where a joint has to carry load or resist chemicals and moisture. Is cured epoxy safe? Once fully cured, epoxy is inert and safe to handle, which is why finished parts pose little risk. The precautions apply to the uncured resin and hardener, which can irritate skin and airways.
